t:
That subsection (b) of section 4 of the Act of November 26, 1969 (83 Stat. 271; 41 U.S.C. 251, note), is amended to read as follows:

“(b) The Commission shall make, on or before December 31, 1972, a final report to the Congress of its findings and its recommendations for changes in statutes, regulations, policies, and procedures designed to carry out the policy stated in section 1 of this Act. In the event the Congress is not in session at the time of submission, the final report shall be submitted to the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate. The Commission may also make such interim reports as it deems advisable.”

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a "Commission" making recommendations signals an advisory body with outside members. But this section only resets the deadline and delivery mechanics for the Commission's final report to Congress, and Congress is inside the federal government. Nothing in the text sets out the Commission's membership, a public hearing, a comment period, consultation with outside parties, or a right to sue.
fable.s: The Commission shall make, on or before December 31, 1972, a final report to the Congress of its findings and its recommendations for changes in statutes, regulations, policies, and procedures

qwen_block.w: This section requires a Commission to submit a report to Congress. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. The definition explicitly excludes reports to Congress or its committees as participation.
qwen_block.s: The Commission shall make, on or before December 31, 1972, a final report to the Congress of its findings and its recommendations

opus.w: This section only amends the deadline and delivery of the Commission's final report to Congress. Reports to Congress, the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate stay inside the federal government, so they are not participation. The tempting reading is that the Commission brings outsiders into policy. But this section says nothing about its membership and requires no consultation, hearing or comment from non-federal parties.
opus.s: The Commission shall make, on or before December 31, 1972, a final report to the Congress of its findings and its recommendations for changes in statutes, regulations, policies, and procedures
opus.b:
I labelled this section **No**. The tempting reading is that a Commission making findings and recommendations brings outsiders into federal policy, so it must be participation. This is likely the Commission on Government Procurement, which had some private members.

That reading fails because this section only changes the deadline and delivery of the Commission's final report to Congress. It says nothing about who sits on the Commission or about any outside input to a federal decision. Under the definition, a report to Congress stays inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires a Commission to submit a report to Congress. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation with outside parties. The definition explicitly states that reports to Congress are not participation.
qwen_chat.s: The Commission shall make, on or before December 31, 1972, a final report to the Congress of its findings and its recommendations for changes in statutes, regulations, policies, and procedures designed to carry out the policy stated in section 1 of this Act.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Commission makes recommendations to Congress, this involves participation. However, Congress is inside the federal government, and reporting to Congress is explicitly listed as a "No" trap in the definition. Furthermore, the section only describes the output (reporting) of the Commission, not the process by which the Commission gathers input from outside parties. The definition requires that the federal government consult or coordinate with people *outside* the government. Reporting to Congress is internal government communication.
